title-group.article-title: Favorable response to second-line sirolimus regardless of STAT3/5b status in acquired pure red cell aplasia: A retrospective study from a single center

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Cyclosporine A (CsA) is the standard first-line treatment for acquired pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), but outcomes vary. Effective salvage strategies for CsA-refractory patients, particularly those with complex secondary subtypes, remain inadequately defined. Additionally, the clinical utility of STAT3/5b mutations in guiding treatment selection remains unclear.

sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: To evaluate the efficacy of second-line sirolimus for the treatment of PRCA and explore the possible genetic predictors for the response.

sec.title: Design
sec.p: This study was a retrospective, single center, comparative study.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Patients with acquired PRCA treated between 2021 and 2025, including 36 patients who received first-line CsA and 22 patients who switched to sirolimus due to lack of response or intolerance. Clinical outcomes, including overall response rate (ORR) and time to response (TTR), were compared between primary and secondary PRCA. STAT3/5b mutation status was also analyzed to assess its predictive value for treatment response.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The ORR for first-line CsA was 25.0% (9/36), with significantly higher efficacy observed in primary cases (42.1%, 8/19) than in secondary cases (5.9%, 1/17; p = 0.015). In the salvage sirolimus group, the ORR was 54.5%, demonstrating efficacy in both primary (37.5%, 3/8) and secondary cases (64.3%, 9/14). The median TTR did not differ significantly between sirolimus and CsA (3.0 vs. 1.5 months, p = 0.150), and both agents achieved sustained remission in responders. Regarding genetic predictors, no responses to CsA were observed in patients harboring STAT3/5b mutations (0/6). In contrast, sirolimus elicited responses in both mutated (3/6) and wild-type (4/5) patients, indicating efficacy irrespective of STAT3/5b status.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: CsA is effective in primary PRCA, whereas sirolimus demonstrates efficacy in both primary and secondary cases regardless of STAT3/5b status. Early genetic profiling may facilitate the identification of patients who may not fully response to CsA and potentially earlier transition to sirolimus salvage therapy.

abstract.title: Plain language summary
abstract.p: Acquired pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is a blood disorder where the body doesn’t make enough red blood cells. Cyclosporine A (CsA) is the usual first treatment, but it doesn’t work well for everyone, especially those with “secondary” PRCA linked to other conditions. In this study, we looked at 36 unique patients treated between 2021-2025. All these patients initially received CsA, and 22 of them subsequently received sirolimus when CsA failed or caused side effects. CsA helped 25% of patients overall, working better for “primary” PRCA (42%) than secondary cases (6%). Sirolimus, used as a second treatment, helped 55% of patients, working well for both primary (38%) and secondary (64%) PRCA. It also worked for patients with certain genetic changes (STAT3/5b mutations) who didn’t respond to CsA. Both drugs took about 1.5-3 months to start working, and benefits lasted in those who responded. However, given the very small genetic subgroups, the observed association between STAT3/5b mutations and treatment response is exploratory. These findings require further validation before genetic profiling can be used to routinely guide treatment selection.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Acquired pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is a rare hematologic syndrome characterized by severe normocytic normochromic anemia, reticulocytopenia, and a selective absence of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, while preserving normal white blood cell and platelet counts. 1 The etiology of this disease is heterogeneous and can be classified into primary and secondary forms. Secondary PRCA is frequently associated with thymoma, lymphoproliferative disorders, particularly T-cell large granular lymphocyte leukemia (T-LGLL), autoimmune diseases, and viral infections (most notably Parvovirus B19).2,3 Its pathogenesis is primarily immune-mediated, involving the suppression of erythropoiesis by cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) or autoantibodies.1,4

Given its autoimmune nature, immunosuppressive therapy (IST) is the standard treatment for acquired PRCA. Currently, cyclosporine A (CsA) is widely accepted as a first-line therapeutic regimen.5,6 Although CsA induces hematologic remission in a substantial proportion of patients, clinical management remains challenging. Long-term use of CsA is often limited by adverse events such as nephrotoxicity, hypertension, hydroelectrolytic imbalances, and gingival hyperplasia. 7 In addition, a subset of patients fails to respond to initial CsA therapy or experiences relapse during maintenance therapy. 8 This issue of treatment failure is particularly pronounced in secondary PRCA, which often exhibits poorer responses to standard IST compared with primary cases. 9 Therefore, effective management strategies for CsA-intolerant or refractory patients represent a significant unmet clinical need.

For patients who fail first-line CsA, there is currently no consensus regarding the optimal salvage therapy. Sirolimus, a mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitor, has emerged as a potential alternative agent.10,11 Unlike CsA, which inhibits calcineurin, sirolimus suppresses T-cell activation via the mTOR signaling pathway. 12 However, data on its use in PRCA patients following CsA failure remain limited to small case series. Furthermore, somatic STAT3 and STAT5b mutations have been well documented in acquired PRCA. 13 These mutations result in constitutive activation of the Janus kinase signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT) signaling pathway, driving aberrant clonal expansion and survival of CTLs, which subsequently destroy erythroid progenitors and inhibit normal erythropoiesis.14,15 Nevertheless, whether these genetic alterations can predict clinical response to CsA or sirolimus remains unclear,16,17 limiting the integration of genetic testing into therapeutic decision-making.

In this single-center retrospective study, the clinical outcomes of patients with acquired PRCA were analyzed. The objectives were to compare the efficacy of first-line CsA in primary versus secondary PRCA, to evaluate the feasibility and efficacy of sirolimus as a salvage therapy for patients with CsA failure or intolerance, and to investigate the association between STAT3/5b mutation status and treatment response. This study aims to provide real-world evidence to support more stratified and individualized treatment strategies for PRCA.

sec.title: Study design and patient enrollment
sec.p: This single-center retrospective cohort study consecutively enrolled hospitalized patients diagnosed with acquired PRCA at the Department of Hematology, Zhejiang Chinese Medical University Hospital, between September 2021 and September 2025. A total of 36 unique patients were included in this study. The cohort included both newly diagnosed patients and those transferred from other institutions with suboptimal responses to unmonitored prior therapies or complex treatment histories. All 36 patients initially received CsA as first-line therapy. Patients were subsequently classified into two groups based on their clinical course. The first-line CsA group continued the initial therapy, whereas the sirolimus salvage group comprised patients who switched to sirolimus due to inefficacy or intolerance. This study was conducted and reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines. 18

sec.title: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
sec.p: Patients were eligible for enrollment if they met all of the following criteria: (1) a confirmed diagnosis of acquired PRCA according to the Chinese Expert Consensus on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Acquired Pure Red Cell Aplasia (2020), 19 defined as a hemoglobin level below the lower limit of normal (males <120 g/L, females <110 g/L), a reticulocyte percentage <1%, and an absolute reticulocyte count <20 × 109/L; (2) receipt of CsA as the first-line treatment at our center, with sirolimus administered exclusively as salvage therapy in cases of CsA refractoriness or intolerance. Patients were required to have a follow-up duration of at least 3 months, except for those who achieved a confirmed hematologic response, including complete response or partial response, or discontinued treatment due to definitive treatment failure or intolerance within the first 3 months; (3) provision of written informed consent.

Patients were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: (1) a diagnosis of congenital or hereditary PRCA, such as Diamond-Blackfan anemia; (2) treatment with antithymocyte globulin (ATG), rituximab, or high-dose corticosteroids defined as >20 mg/day prednisone equivalent for more than 4 weeks within 3 months prior to enrollment, or concurrent use of other potent immunosuppressants, including but not limited to tacrolimus, cyclophosphamide, or low-dose weekly methotrexate. Patients who discontinued these agents due to inefficacy, defined as a hemoglobin increase <30 g/L after 3 months, or intolerance, defined as Grade ≥3 toxicity according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (NCI CTCAE), were also excluded if the washout period was less than 2 weeks, although prior short-term low-dose corticosteroid use was permitted. However, to evaluate the independent clinical efficacy of target immunosuppressive therapies, patients receiving concurrent steroid treatment were excluded to eliminate potential confounding factors on erythropoiesis; (3) presence of severe cardiac, hepatic, or renal dysfunction, or pregnancy or lactation; and (4) loss to follow-up within 3 months without documented hematologic improvement. These patients were excluded from the efficacy analysis due to indeterminate outcomes. However, patients who achieved complete response or partial response within 3 months but were subsequently lost to follow-up were classified as responders. In such cases, the duration of response (DOR) was censored at the date of the last available follow-up.

sec.title: CsA as first-line therapy
sec.p: CsA was administered orally at an initial dose of 3 to 5 mg/kg/day. The dosage was adjusted based on therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) to maintain a target whole-blood trough concentration of 150 to 200 ng/mL. For patients transferred from other centers who were already receiving ongoing CsA therapy with suboptimal responses, CsA was continued and optimized strictly under TDM at our center. Patients were definitively classified as CsA-refractory and transitioned to sirolimus only after failing to respond to an optimized, TDM-guided CsA regimen.

sec.title: Sirolimus as salvage therapy
sec.p: For patients who transitioned to sirolimus due to CsA failure or intolerance, treatment was typically initiated at 2 mg/day, followed by a maintenance dose of 1 to 3 mg/day. The dosage was adjusted to maintain a target whole-blood trough concentration of 2 to 4 ng/mL.

sec.title: Maintenance and tapering regimens
sec.p: For patients who achieved a stable CR or PR, the effective therapeutic dosage of CsA or sirolimus was typically maintained for at least 6 months. Following this maintenance phase, a slow and individualized tapering process was initiated if the disease remained stable. The tapering period typically spanned 1 to 2 years. Depending on individual disease stability and drug tolerance, some patients required indefinite treatment with a minimal maintenance dose to sustain hematologic remission.

sec.title: Response criteria and efficacy assessment
sec.p: Treatment response was evaluated according to the Chinese Expert Consensus (2020) criteria. To accurately assess treatment efficacy and exclude the transient effects of exogenous blood, hematological response was evaluated at least 4 weeks after the last red blood cell (RBC) transfusion. Complete remission (CR) was defined as normalization of hemoglobin levels (males >120 g/L, females >110 g/L), accompanied by normal white blood cell (WBC) and platelet counts. Partial remission (PR) was defined as a hemoglobin increase of >30 g/L from baseline or achievement of transfusion independence, accompanied by normal WBC and platelet counts. No response (NR) was defined as failure to meet the criteria for PR.

The primary efficacy endpoint was the overall response rate (ORR). Secondary endpoints included the prevalence of STAT3/5b mutations, time to response (TTR), and DOR. Safety assessments focused on drug-specific adverse events, particularly CsA-induced nephrotoxicity and hypertension, as well as sirolimus-associated hyperlipidemia and mucositis. TTR was defined as the interval from the initiation of the respective immunosuppressive therapy (CsA or sirolimus) to the first documentation of CR or PR. For patients who did not achieve hematologic improvement or discontinued treatment due to lack of efficacy, TTR was recorded as NR in the final analysis. For patients who achieved a confirmed hematologic response but had irregular follow-up intervals resulting in delayed documentation, the exact TTR could not be accurately determined. These patients were included in the ORR analysis but excluded from the calculation of median TTR to minimize statistical bias.

sec.title: Mutational analysis
sec.p: Genetic mutation profiles were retrospectively collected from patients’ historical next-generation sequencing (NGS) reports, based on either hematological targeted panels (e.g., the MDS/AA 85-gene and 63+49-gene panels) or whole-exome sequencing (WES). Patients whose NGS panels did not explicitly cover STAT3 and STAT5b were classified as untested and excluded from the mutational analysis. For patients evaluated with WES or panels incorporating these specific targets, the STAT3/5b status was defined as wild-type in the absence of detectable variants, and as mutated if corresponding variants were identified.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data were analyzed using SPSS Statistics 27.0. Normally distributed continuous variables are presented as mean ± standard deviation, whereas non-normally distributed variables are presented as median (range). Normality was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Between-group comparisons were performed using the independent samples t-test for normally distributed data, the Mann-Whitney U test for non-normally distributed data, and the chi-square test for categorical variables. All statistical tests were two-sided, and a P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For variables with missing values, cases were excluded only from the specific analyses involving those variables, and no data imputation was performed.

sec.title: Ethics approval and consent to participate
sec.p: This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (No. 2025-KLS-1036-01, Date: 05/01/2026). All procedures involving human participants were conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional research committee and with the 1964 Helsinki Declaration and its subsequent amendments or comparable ethical standards. All participants provided written informed consent at enrollment, agreeing to the use of their anonymized data for research purposes in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: Patient enrollment and baseline characteristics
sec.p:
Of the 55 patients with acquired PRCA screened for the first-line CsA treatment group, 19 were excluded, resulting in a final cohort of 36 patients (Figure 1). Four patients in this cohort subsequently discontinued CsA treatment due to intolerance and were directly allocated to the sirolimus salvage therapy group. The study population included 21 patients initially diagnosed at our center and 15 patients previously managed at other institutions. For the latter group, baseline data at the time of initial diagnosis were retrospectively collected from external medical records and were relatively limited. Therefore, baseline laboratory parameters were analyzed based solely on the 21 newly diagnosed patients. Genetic testing was completed in 17 patients, with STAT3/5b mutations detected in 6 cases. Comprehensive patient demographics, clinical classifications, and baseline laboratory characteristics are detailed in Table 1.Figure 1.

sec.title: Treatment response
sec.p:
Among the 36 patients who received first-line CsA, four discontinued treatment early due to intolerance. In accordance with standard clinical evaluation principles, these patients were classified as treatment failures (non-responders) and included in the efficacy evaluation. Among the 36 evaluable patients, 6 (16.7%) achieved CR and 3 (8.3%) achieved PR, yielding an ORR of 25.0% (Figure 2). The remaining 27 patients (75.0%), including the 4 intolerant cases, exhibited NR. No significant differences were observed among response groups with respect to sex distribution (p = 0.146), age (p = 0.529), or hemoglobin levels (p = 0.093). Of the 22 patients treated with sirolimus, CR and PR were each observed in 6 patients (27.3%), while 10 patients (45.5%) exhibited NR, resulting in an ORR of 54.5% (Figure 2). The efficacy of sirolimus was not significantly associated with sex (p = 0.494), baseline age (p = 0.920), or hemoglobin level (p = 0.251).Figure 2.
Patient flow and treatment outcomes in acquired PRCA. The Sankey diagram illustrates the clinical course of 36 patients treated with first-line Cyclosporine A (CsA). Patients who showed no response (NR) or intolerance to CsA (left side) proceeded to Sirolimus salvage therapy (middle flow), resulting in the final outcomes depicted on the right. The width of the bands is proportional to the number of patients.

Further analysis based on the mutation status were performed, showing that among the 11 patients with wild-type STAT3/5b in the CsA group, 3 achieved CR and 1 achieved PR. The 2 patients who discontinued treatment due to intolerance were classified as NR, bringing the total number of non-responders in this subgroup to 7, resulting in a response rate of 36.3% (4/11). In contrast, none of the six patients harboring STAT3/5b mutations responded to CsA (Figure 3(a)). In the sirolimus group, among the five patients with wild-type STAT3/5b, four responded, including one with CR and three with PR, yielding a response rate of 80%. Furthermore, among the six patients with STAT3/5b mutations, three responded, corresponding to a response rate of 50% (Figure 3(b)). No statistically significant association was observed between STAT3/5b mutation status and response to either CsA or sirolimus (p > 0.05). However, the observed trend suggests that STAT3/5b mutations may be associated with reduced responsiveness to CsA, whereas sirolimus may still induce therapeutic responses in a subset of patients harboring these mutations. This finding warrants further validation in larger studies.Figure 3.
Impact of STAT3/5b gene mutation status on clinical response to cyclosporine A and sirolimus. (A) Response rates to first-line cyclosporine A (CsA) stratified by STAT3/5b mutation status (n=17). No clinical response was observed in patients harboring STAT3/5b mutations (0/6, 0%), whereas STAT3/5b wild-type patients achieved an overall response rate of 44.4% (4/9). Two wild-type patients discontinued treatment due to intolerance and were excluded from the efficacy calculation. (B) Response rates to sirolimus salvage therapy stratified by STAT3/5b mutation status (n=11). In the sirolimus cohort, efficacy was observed regardless of mutation status, with response rates of 50% (3/6) in STAT3/5b mutated patients and 80% (4/5) in wild-type patients.

sec.title: Treatment outcomes in primary vs secondary PRCA
sec.p:
Among the 19 patients with primary PRCA treated with CsA, 6 achieved CR and 2 achieved PR, while the 3 patients who discontinued management due to intolerance were evaluated as treatment failures. Most responders demonstrated an increase in hemoglobin levels above 100 g/L within 3 months. In contrast, outcomes were poor in the secondary PRCA group (n = 17). In this subgroup, the majority patients were diagnosed with T-LGLL (n = 15), while one case was associated with thymoma and one with other etiologies. The only responder in this subgroup was a patient with T-LGLL who achieved PR (Figure 4(a)). The distribution of responses differed significantly between subtypes (p = 0.015). This disparity, largely attributable to the refractory nature of the T-LGLL subgroup, accounts for the low overall response rate observed in the entire cohort.Figure 4.
Comparison of clinical response to cyclosporine A and sirolimus based on PRCA classification. (A) Response rates to first-line cyclosporine A (CsA) stratified by disease subtype (primary vs. secondary PRCA). Patients with primary PRCA (n=19) demonstrated a significantly superior response rate compared to those with secondary PRCA (n=17) (p = 0.015). Three patients in the primary group discontinued treatment due to intolerance. (B) Response rates to sirolimus salvage therapy stratified by disease subtype. In the secondary PRCA cohort (n=14, predominantly associated with T-LGLL), sirolimus elicited complete or partial remissions in 9 patients, despite prior CsA failure. Among patients with primary PRCA (n=8), 3 achieved partial remission. No statistically significant difference in overall response rate was observed between the two subgroups (p = 0.378).

Sirolimus demonstrated substantial efficacy in the subgroup in which CsA had failed. Among the 14 patients with secondary PRCA, predominantly associated with T-LGLL, 9 responded, including 6 with CR and 3 with PR, yielding an ORR of 64.3%. Among the 8 patients with primary PRCA, 3 achieved PR, corresponding to an ORR of 37.5% (Figure 4(b)). Although this difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.378), likely due to the limited sample size, these findings suggest that sirolimus represents an effective salvage therapy, particularly for T-LGLL-associated PRCA refractory to CsA.

Furthermore, to explore the biological rationale behind this efficacy, we cross-analyzed the T-LGLL diagnosis with STAT mutational status and treatment outcomes. Strikingly, STAT mutations were highly enriched in this subgroup, with 5 out of 8 (62.5%) tested T-LGLL patients harboring STAT3/5b mutations. Clinically, this specific cohort exhibited uniform resistance to frontline CsA (0/8 responded), regardless of their mutational status. However, when 7 of these refractory patients subsequently received sirolimus salvage therapy, robust responses were observed across the board. Among the 5 patients with STAT mutations, 3 responded (1 CR, 2 PR, 2 NR); interestingly, both of the 2 patients with wild-type STAT also responded (1 CR, 1 PR). These findings strongly support the hypothesis that sirolimus effectively targets the underlying T-cell pathogenesis in T-LGLL-associated PRCA, overcoming initial CsA resistance and yielding substantial clinical benefit regardless of the specific STAT mutational status.

sec.title: Time to response (TTR) and duration of response (DOR)
sec.p:
The TTR was evaluated to assess the onset speed of therapeutic efficacy. Patients responding to first-line CsA (N = 9) achieved a median TTR of 1.5 months (range: 1 to 7 months). In the salvage setting, the median TTR for sirolimus was numerically longer at 3.0 months (range: 2 to 9 months), although this difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.150) (Figure 5). To minimize analytical bias caused by irregular outpatient monitoring, three responding patients in the sirolimus group with unusually prolonged documented onset times (11, 17, and 19 months) due to delayed follow-up visits were excluded from this specific TTR calculation. Consequently, the TTR analysis for sirolimus included 9 patients (N = 9). Importantly, further subgroup analyses revealed that neither the disease etiology (primary vs. secondary) nor the STAT3/5b mutation status significantly impacted the TTR in either treatment arm (all p > 0.05). These findings indicate that although sirolimus has a slightly longer response time, it effectively improves blood counts in a wide range of patients.Figure 5.
Individual patient dynamics of treatment response and follow-up duration. Each horizontal bar represents a single patient’s timeline. Patients are stratified by treatment group: Blue bars represent the CsA group, and orange bars represent the Sirolimus group. The markers indicate the time to initial therapeutic response (Onset). Triangles denote CsA onset, and circles denote Sirolimus onset. Arrows at the end of bars indicate patients with an ongoing response at the time of data cutoff. Flat ends indicate observation termination due to loss to follow-up. The specific onset markers for PT14, PT15, and PT21 are not displayed. Because of irregular follow-up intervals, their exact TTR could not be accurately determined due to significantly delayed documentation.

Regarding the DOR, both immunosuppressive agents demonstrated highly durable disease control once an initial response was achieved. Strikingly, no relapses were observed in either the CsA or sirolimus groups during the observation period. Consequently, the median DOR was not reached for any cohort or subgroup. Responders in the CsA group maintained continuous remission with a median follow-up of 7.0 months (range: 1 to 41 months). Similarly, responders in the sirolimus salvage group exhibited sustained efficacy with a median follow-up of 16.5 months (range: 1 to 47 months) (Figure 5). The subset of patients harboring STAT3/5b mutations maintained durable remission for a median of 32.0 months. These results highlight that while CsA effectively sustains remission in primary PRCA, sirolimus delivers equally durable disease control for high-risk patients, effectively rescuing those with secondary etiologies or STAT3/5b mutations.

For patients who achieved a stable therapeutic response, the daily dosage of CsA or sirolimus was gradually tapered in an individualized manner. This de-escalation was guided by TDM. The goal was to reach the minimum daily maintenance dose required to sustain the target whole-blood trough concentrations (150 to 200 ng/mL for CsA and 2 to 4 ng/mL for sirolimus) while minimizing drug-related toxicity. During the tapering phase, minor hematological fluctuations were promptly managed by temporary dose re-escalation. Because these fluctuations were successfully rescued by routine dose adjustments without requiring a change in the line of therapy, they were not classified as definitive clinical relapses. This proactive TDM-guided management, combined with the relatively short median follow-up period, explains the absence of documented relapses in this cohort.

sec.title: Concomitant supportive care
sec.p: Most patients received concurrent hematopoietic supportive care to manage severe anemia. In the CsA cohort, commonly administered supportive therapies included androgens, such as testosterone undecanoate, and erythropoietin (EPO). Similarly, in the sirolimus salvage group, 31.8% of patients received a combination of sirolimus, androgens, and EPO, while an additional 40.9% received sirolimus in combination with either androgens or EPO alone. While EPO is ineffective during the acute aplastic phase when target erythroblasts are absent, it was administered in our cohort to support and accelerate erythroid proliferation during the hematopoietic recovery phase, particularly after immunosuppressive treatments began to take effect. Furthermore, this supportive use was guided by the regular monitoring of serum EPO concentrations. These agents were administered as supportive measures to reduce transfusion dependence while awaiting the therapeutic effects of immunosuppressive treatment. Two patients with significant iron overload also received deferasirox.

sec.title: Safety observation
sec.p: In the CsA group (n = 36), documented adverse events were relatively infrequent. Five patients (13.9%) experienced hepatic or renal impairment, whereas oral ulcers and urinary tract infections were each observed in one patient (2.8%).

In the sirolimus group (n = 22), infectious complications were the predominant adverse events. Pulmonary infections, specifically pneumonia, occurred in seven patients (31.8%), among whom several experienced recurrent episodes during the follow-up period. One patient (4.5%) with a history of recurrent pneumonia and poorly controlled blood pressure developed tuberculous meningitis. Another patient (4.5%) presented with pleural effusion in the context of pneumonia. Non-infectious adverse events were less common, with gastrointestinal dysfunction and tooth loosening each occurring in one patient (4.5%).

Due to the retrospective nature of this study, adverse events in the remaining patients were not comprehensively documented. All reported adverse events were managed with dose adjustment or supportive care.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This retrospective cohort study primarily evaluated the efficacy of sirolimus as a salvage therapy for acquired PRCA, while also assessing the outcomes of standard first-line CsA treatment in a real-world tertiary care setting. The most notable finding is that sirolimus achieved an ORR of 54.5% in patients who were refractory or intolerant to CsA. This efficacy was particularly evident in patients with PRCA secondary to T-LGLL. Furthermore, exploratory genetic analysis suggested that although STAT3/5b mutations may be associated with poor responses to CsA, sirolimus retained therapeutic activity in this mutation-positive subgroup.

The overall ORR for first-line CsA in this study was 25.0%, which is lower than the 60 to 80% reported in previous studies. 5 We propose two main clinical factors to explain this discrepancy. First, this difference is heavily attributable to referral bias. As the data were derived from a tertiary referral center, the cohort included a substantial proportion of patients transferred from other institutions. Many of these patients were admitted with ongoing but suboptimally managed CsA therapy from local hospitals. These patients inherently had a worse prognosis and a higher likelihood of ultimate CsA failure compared with newly diagnosed, treatment-naive patients. Second, we applied a strict intention-to-treat approach, classifying patients who discontinued CsA early due to drug intolerance as treatment failures. This conservative method yields a lower statistical ORR but provides a highly realistic reflection of real-world clinical challenges. This high refractory burden is particularly evident in the marked difference in CsA efficacy observed between primary PRCA (ORR 42.1%) and PRCA secondary to T-LGLL (ORR <10%). Although CsA remains a standard first-line treatment for T-LGLL, the poor outcomes observed in the secondary cohort highlight the clinical challenges associated with refractory T-LGLL, thereby underscoring the need for alternative therapeutic options. Previous studies have demonstrated the efficacy of sirolimus in refractory PRCA and T-LGLL.10,20,21 The observed ORR of 54.5% in this pretreated population further supports the role of sirolimus as an effective second-line therapy.

The difference in CsA efficacy between primary and secondary PRCA underscores the heterogeneity of PRCA pathogenesis. CsA exerts its immunosuppressive effects primarily through inhibition of calcineurin, thereby blocking the nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT) signaling pathway and suppressing interleukin-2 production. 22 This mechanism is particularly effective in primary autoimmune PRCA, in which T-cell dysregulation is typically mediated through conventional activation pathways.1,8,20 The present findings are consistent with this mechanism, as response rates were significantly higher in primary PRCA than in secondary forms. In contrast, the poor response to CsA in secondary PRCA suggests the involvement of alternative pathogenic mechanisms that are not dependent on calcineurin signaling. Moreover, therapeutic success in secondary PRCA is often dependent on effective control of the underlying disease. Since CsA primarily acts as a symptomatic immunosuppressant, its inability to eliminate the primary pathogenic driver may limit its efficacy as monotherapy in this subgroup.

The efficacy of sirolimus as a salvage therapy may be attributed to its distinct mechanism of action. As an mTOR inhibitor, sirolimus targets the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B/mTOR (PI3K/AKT/mTOR) signaling pathway, which plays a critical role in regulating cell proliferation and survival. 23 In secondary PRCA subtypes, particularly T-LGLL, constitutive activation of the STAT3 pathway is a recognized driver of clonal expansion.13,24,25 Although mechanistic investigations were not conducted in this study, the observed trend, in which patients harboring STAT3/5b mutations were refractory to CsA but responsive to sirolimus, supports a plausible pharmacological hypothesis. Constitutive activation of STAT3/5b may reduce the dependence of pathogenic T cells on calcineurin signaling, thereby contributing to CsA resistance, whereas inhibition of the mTOR pathway may circumvent this mechanism.

In this study, the TTR did not differ significantly between the two treatment groups, with a median of 1.5 months for CsA and 3.0 months for sirolimus (p = 0.150). The response kinetics of sirolimus are consistent with its mechanism of action as an mTOR inhibitor, reflecting a gradual process of clonal suppression rather than immediate cytokine inhibition. Responders in the CsA group maintained continuous remission throughout the observation period. Similarly, patients in the sirolimus group achieved sustained disease control without documented relapse. This observation was particularly evident in patients with STAT3/5b mutations. Despite a relatively delayed onset of response, these patients maintained remission throughout follow-up. These findings suggest that, in patients with mutation-positive or refractory PRCA, sirolimus may serve not only as a bridging therapy but also as a definitive treatment capable of achieving long-term disease control. However, the precise biological role of STAT3/5b mutations remains to be fully elucidated. These observations should therefore be interpreted with caution and require validation in future mechanistic studies and larger clinical cohorts.16,17

These findings support a stratified, precision medicine approach to the management of PRCA. First, distinguishing between primary and secondary PRCA is essential. Although CsA is an appropriate first-line therapy for primary PRCA, its limited efficacy in secondary cases suggests that alternative strategies should be considered earlier in the disease course for this subgroup. Sirolimus demonstrated favorable efficacy in both primary and secondary PRCA. Given the uniform CsA resistance observed in specific subgroups, our findings suggest that the clinical utility of sirolimus may extend beyond a strict second-line salvage role. For patients with secondary etiologies (such as T-LGLL) or those harboring STAT mutations, introducing sirolimus earlier in the treatment algorithm could be a reasonable and targeted clinical consideration. However, larger prospective studies are required to definitively confirm its safety and efficacy as an upfront frontline therapy. Second, the potential predictive value of STAT3/5b mutations warrants consideration. However, given the very small genetic subgroups and the absence of statistically significant associations, the observed association between STAT3/5b mutations and treatment response is exploratory and hypothesis-generating and requires validation before genetic profiling can be used to guide treatment selection. Third, based on the median TTR of 3.0 months observed for sirolimus in this study, clinicians should consider maintaining treatment for at least 3 to 6 months to adequately assess therapeutic efficacy and avoid premature discontinuation.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, as a single-center retrospective study, the findings are subject to selection bias. Specifically, many patients were transferred after suboptimal responses to unmonitored ongoing CsA therapy at local hospitals. These patients inherently carried a worse prognosis than newly diagnosed cases, which likely contributed to the relatively low overall response rate in our CsA cohort. Second, the sample size, especially within the genetic analysis subgroup, was limited, thereby reducing the statistical power to definitively establish the association between STAT3/5b mutations and treatment response. Third, due to the retrospective nature of this study and the frequent transfer of patients from primary hospitals, precise quantitative baseline bone marrow differential counts were unavailable for a subset of the cohort. Nevertheless, the diagnosis in these patients was stringently verified through comprehensive clinical records and bone marrow biopsy summaries. Finally, the retrospective nature of data collection precluded a standardized assessment of long-term relapse rates. Furthermore, outpatient follow-up intervals for blood tests were not strictly standardized. This irregular monitoring schedule introduces a potential analytical bias. It limits the highly precise evaluation of TTR and remains an inherent limitation of our real-world setting.

sec.title: Future directions
sec.p: Although CsA remains an effective first-line treatment for primary PRCA, the results highlight its limitations in cases associated with T-LGLL, particularly in refractory settings. Sirolimus demonstrates substantial efficacy as a salvage therapy in this population, addressing an important unmet clinical need. The differential treatment response according to STAT3/5b mutation status provides a rationale for incorporating genetic profiling into the diagnostic evaluation. The presence of these mutations is associated with a high likelihood of CsA resistance and a favorable long-term response to sirolimus, supporting their use in guiding patients toward targeted salvage therapy earlier in the disease course. Future prospective, multicenter studies with larger cohorts are required to validate these biomarker-driven therapeutic strategies.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Altogether, sirolimus demonstrates efficacy in both primary and secondary cases regardless of STAT3/5b status. While still exploratory, early genetic profiling may potentially facilitate the identification of patients who may not fully respond to CsA, warranting further validation for its use in guiding earlier transition to sirolimus salvage therapy.
